opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing I'd want to do is pull apart some of the things that are currently all tangled together inside these models. Right now a single large language model is doing at least three quite different jobs at once. It's acting as a model of language, so it knows grammar, discourse, and how to produce fluent text. It's acting as a knowledge base, storing an enormous number of facts about the world in its weights. And it's doing some kind of reasoning or problem solving on top of that. Because everything lives in the same set of parameters, we get many of the problems people complain about. The model hallucinates because it can't distinguish what it actually knows from what merely sounds plausible. It's very hard to update when the world changes, because you can't just go in and edit a fact. And it's hard to attribute an answer to a source.

So the modular approach I'd advocate starts with separating linguistic competence from factual knowledge. Let the language component be very good at understanding questions and generating answers, but have it consult an explicit, external knowledge store for the facts, whether that's a knowledge graph, a document collection, or some structured database. Retrieval-augmented generation is a step in that direction, but I think we can go further. If the knowledge is held explicitly, you can update it, audit it, check its provenance, and know when it's missing something.

The second piece I'd emphasize is what I'd call metacognition: modules that monitor the system's own competence. A well-engineered system should know when it's outside its competence, when its uncertainty is high, when a question touches something it doesn't have good knowledge about. That suggests having components that estimate epistemic uncertainty and can say "I don't know," or "let me go look that up," instead of confabulating.

Third, I'd look at the cognitive science literature for inspiration. Human cognition seems to have fairly distinct subsystems: episodic memory for specific events, semantic memory for general knowledge, working memory, planning, and so on. LLMs currently lack a real episodic memory. They can't remember what happened in a previous interaction and learn from it in a controlled way. Building explicit modules for those functions, with clean interfaces between them, could give us systems that are more reliable and easier to maintain.

And finally, from an engineering point of view, modularity is just good practice. Every mature engineering discipline builds systems out of components with well-defined specifications that can be tested independently. Today we have these giant monolithic models where, if something goes wrong, the only remedy is more training data or more fine-tuning, with uncertain side effects elsewhere. If we can decompose them into parts with clear responsibilities, we can test each part, verify it, and replace it when needed. That's the path toward systems we can actually trust in high-stakes applications.

r001.rationale: The response proposes separating factual knowledge from the model and storing it in an explicit external knowledge store, including a knowledge graph or structured database.

r002.rationale: It discusses modular components and testing them independently but does not identify preserving end-to-end training as a constraint.

r003.rationale: It does not propose withholding knowledge-base entries for facts that can be inferred from existing knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that the current approach of building one gigantic monolithic network and training it end to end on everything is, in my view, a dead end, at least as a long-term architecture. It's an engineering nightmare. If you want to update a single fact, you have to retrain or fine-tune the whole thing, and you can't verify what happened. So I've been arguing that we should think of the large language model as a component in a larger system, not as the system itself.

The core idea is to separate the parts that should be stable from the parts that should change. The thing that the language model is really good at is language. It knows syntax, it knows how to compose sentences, it knows discourse structure, and it has a sort of broad, fuzzy competence at reasoning. What it's bad at is being a database. Factual knowledge about the world is exactly the thing that changes constantly, and it's the thing we most want to be able to inspect, correct, and attribute to sources. So one way to approach modularity is to try to pull the factual knowledge out of the weights and put it into an external knowledge base, a retrieval system, a set of documents, maybe a structured knowledge graph, and then train the language model to consult that store rather than memorize it.

Now, that's easy to say and hard to do, because right now those two things are completely entangled in the parameters. One research direction I'm interested in is whether you can train the model in such a way that it is actually discouraged from memorizing facts, so that it is forced to look them up. If you can succeed at that, you get a model that is smaller, more stable, and whose knowledge you can update by editing a document rather than by running a training job.

The second piece is reasoning and planning. We've seen that chain-of-thought prompting helps, but it's still the same network doing everything. I'd rather see explicit modules, perhaps a planner, perhaps a verifier, perhaps calls out to tools like a theorem prover or a Python interpreter, where the language model acts as a kind of interface and orchestrator. That's the way the rest of software engineering works. We don't build an operating system as one undifferentiated blob. We have components with interfaces, and we can test them independently.

And the third piece, which I think is underappreciated, is epistemic. A modular system can tell you where a claim came from. If the answer is retrieved from a document, you can cite it. If it came out of a reasoning module, you can show the steps. A monolithic model just produces fluent text, and fluency is not the same as truth. So modularity isn't only about engineering convenience. It's about being able to trust and maintain these systems over time.

r001.rationale: It proposes moving factual knowledge out of the model’s weights into an external knowledge base, including a structured knowledge graph.

r002.rationale: It criticizes end-to-end training as part of a monolithic approach and advocates explicit modules; it does not identify preserving end-to-end training as a constraint.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss withholding knowledge-base entries when facts can be inferred from existing knowledge.

astra-6.text:
I would start by asking what we want to be able to change independently. In a large language model, knowledge and the procedures for using that knowledge are all mixed together in the weights. That makes it difficult to update one fact or improve one capability without potentially affecting something else.

One approach is to move some of that knowledge outside the model. The language model can formulate a query, retrieve information, and reason with what comes back. Similarly, when it needs to do a calculation, it can call a calculator or a program. Those give us components that we can test and update separately.

But the harder question is how to get modularity inside the learned system. You could imagine having different modules for different kinds of reasoning, with a controller that decides which ones to invoke. The challenge is defining the interfaces: What does one module communicate to another, and how do we train them so that replacing one doesn't require retraining the whole system?

So I would pursue explicit tools and external memory as a practical starting point, while investigating how to learn components with stable interfaces. Simply dividing a network into pieces doesn't necessarily give you the independence that makes modularity useful.

r001.rationale: The response proposes external memory and retrieval, but does not specify storing factual knowledge in a knowledge graph or database.

r002.rationale: It says replacing a module should not require retraining the whole system, but does not identify preserving end-to-end training as a constraint.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss withholding knowledge-base entries when facts can be inferred from existing knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would start by asking what we want the modules to do. One possibility is to have a language model act as an interface to a collection of specialized components—a planner, a database, a theorem prover, or a simulator. The language model helps interpret the request, but it can hand off parts of the problem to components whose behavior we understand and can test independently.

The harder question is how to define the interfaces. What information does one module pass to another? How does it express uncertainty? And how do we know whether a failure came from choosing the wrong module, supplying the wrong inputs, or getting an incorrect result back?

So I would probably begin with relatively explicit interfaces and separately trained components. Then we could investigate how much to learn jointly. The attraction is that you could improve or replace one capability without retraining the entire system. But you have to demonstrate that the decomposition actually makes the system more reliable and easier to maintain.
